prompt:
[Game] Urban-Fantasy Action RPG with Dual Day/Night Loop: During the day, build interpersonal bonds at an academy; at night, infiltrate other people's fractured memory realms and fight. Advanced powers require sacrificing your own memories, and every deleted memory simultaneously rewrites available story content, bond routes, and combat abilities—character-development resources are narrative resources.
[Core Mechanics] Daytime social system: at least six interactable characters, each with a persistent bond level advanced through dialogue choices, gifts, and shared events; bond levels unlock corresponding nighttime combo abilities. Nighttime combat: enter character-generated memory realms (at least three), using real-time action combat layered with time abilities—short rewind (undo damage and displacement taken by the player within the last few seconds), brief enemy stasis, and a temporal echo that replays the player's attack sequence from the previous few seconds. Memory sacrifice: permanently delete one of your own memories in exchange for an advanced skill; dialogue choices, side stories, and bond routes tied to the deleted memory close or downgrade permanently, with no recovery. Combo economy: combo abilities consume resonance accumulated through the corresponding character's bond; deeper bonds make combos stronger, and resonance recovers through daytime interaction and nighttime cooperative kills. Win/loss loop: repair at least three memory realms to reach the finale; if the stock of humanizing memories falls below a threshold, trigger the Lost Self ending; the calendar lasts at least fourteen days, with limited day/night action points forcing tradeoffs.
[Must Implement] Direct mapping between bond progression and combo unlocks; three time powers—rewind, stasis, echo; permanent memory sacrifice and its bidirectional rewriting of story accessibility and combat ability; resonance consumption and recovery economy; a cross-system cascade such as sacrificing a memory tied to a character → that character's bond route downgrades → corresponding combo becomes unavailable; identical replay results when rewinding within the same battle.

desc: 改史者对弈：事件卡打进时间线依赖图激起涟漪重算，悖论会被判定器抓住，AI对手在同一条时间线上拆你的前置
prompt:
[Game] History-Rewriter Duel: A strategy card game where Event Cards are played into a timeline to rewrite history. Every card sends ripples forward through an event-dependency graph, paradoxes are caught by a validator, and your opponent is rewriting the same timeline.
[Core Mechanics] The timeline is an event-dependency graph containing at least fifteen event nodes arranged along a time axis, with at least four dependency types: prerequisite, mutually exclusive, bonus, and trigger. Some nodes provide ongoing benefits to their controller, such as extra time energy each turn. Playing Event Cards can insert, remove, or move nodes; changes propagate step by step along dependency edges into the future and recompute downstream state, with the ripple visualized on the timeline. Economy: at least thirty Event Cards each have a time-energy cost. Energy restores by turn, hands replenish by turn, and cards cannot be played without enough energy, forcing tradeoffs between high-impact changes and hand tempo. Paradox validation: if a change creates a missing prerequisite or cyclic dependency, a paradox triggers a timed stabilization phase with a quick puzzle. Success preserves the timeline; failure degrades that segment and adds one paradox count. Opponent AI: one local AI rewriter also plays cards each turn to modify the same graph, pursuing an end-state goal that conflicts with the player's and removing prerequisite nodes from the player's target events. Win if the timeline end-state satisfies your objective within the turn limit; lose after three unstabilized paradoxes or if the AI reaches its goal first. With the same seed and same card sequence, the final timeline state must match.
[Must Implement] Dependency propagation/recomputation and ripple visualization; cost, energy, and hand economy constraints; paradox trigger → stabilization → degradation loop; AI and player edits propagating through the same dependency graph; win/loss logic; identical final state for the same seed.
[Creative Freedom] Card themes (invention, rescue, disaster), chain combos, era-layered visuals, and additional dependency types are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.
[Mobile] This game targets mobile browsers: choose either portrait or landscape and lock the orientation; all interaction must be touch-only; any hover, keyboard, mouse, or other desktop interaction mentioned in the prompt must be implemented with a touch-equivalent interaction; support mainstream mobile resolutions and safe areas while maintaining smooth performance on mobile devices.

desc: 怪兽卡市：元素克制牌局与卡牌行情双循环——战绩推高行情、行情决定牌力，你既是牌手也是投机商
prompt:
[Game] Monster Card Market: A buy-low, sell-high elemental monster-card survival game where market prices fluctuate with events and your battle record. Every victory at the card table rewrites market prices—you are both a duelist and a speculator.
[Core Mechanics] Combat system: at least twenty monster cards belong to five elements—fire, water, earth, electricity, and wind—and form a counter loop (fire beats earth, water beats fire, earth beats electricity, electricity beats water, while wind serves as a balancing element). Cards are played in turns, and the advantaged element deals significantly higher damage. Each card has attack, health, rarity, and a special effect, with at least four rarity tiers. Opponents are a sequence of increasingly strong AI card players. Battle rewards fluctuate with opponent difficulty and victory efficiency—the harder the opponent and the cleaner the win, the greater the payout. Market system: each card's price fluctuates around a rarity-based baseline, driven by at least six categories of market events such as an element rally, supply crisis, or rare flash sale. The player's battle record feeds back into prices: repeatedly winning with an element raises the market value of cards from that element. The shop supports buying and selling, and profiting from spreads is a survival path equal to battling. The two systems are interlocked: market prices determine which cards you can afford, decks determine which battles you can win, and selling a core card for cash immediately weakens combat strength, making the timing of liquidation a central decision. Money is the only lifeline: reaching the target asset value wins, while reaching zero cash with insufficient card value to continue causes defeat. Event sequence and initial prices are consistent for the same seed.
[Must Implement] Elemental counter loop applied in damage resolution; rarity baseline plus event-driven price fluctuations; feedback from battle record into market prices; battle rewards linked to difficulty and efficiency; a closed buy/sell loop that permits positive spread profit; win/loss logic and same-seed consistency.
[Creative Freedom] Card-effect systems, win-streak rewards, black markets, auctions, and collection catalogs are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.

desc: 级联赛跑电网抢修：一座变电站烧毁只是开始——负载重分配的连锁过载在图上逐跳蔓延，你调度抢修车与传播速度赛跑
prompt:
[Game] Urban Grid Emergency-Repair Dispatch Simulation: On a thunderstorm night in Echo City, one burned substation is only the beginning—its load shifts onto neighboring nodes and triggers cascading overloads. You dispatch repair trucks across the road network in a race against propagation: repair quickly and you are a hero; repair slowly and you become the cause of the next, larger blackout.
[Core Mechanics] Power-grid topology simulation: hundreds of nodes—power plants, substations, and transformers—and lines form a graph. When a node fails, its load transfers by rule to adjacent available nodes; nodes that exceed capacity burn out after a defined delay, creating hop-by-hop cascade propagation. Failure generation: a thunderstorm corridor moves according to the seed, with strike probability positively correlated with equipment age; overload, aging, and lightning are three distinguishable fault causes. Repair dispatch: multiple engineering vehicles travel across the city road network with travel time, and repairs occupy time. Concurrent failures require prioritization, while critical buildings such as hospitals have blackout deadlines. Economy and upgrades: income and reputation are awarded based on restoration speed and power continuity for critical buildings, and can be spent on additional vehicles/tools, line capacity upgrades, and redundant loop networks—capacity expansion directly changes the propagation surface of future cascades. Chapter loop: each chapter contains one major outage event, with progression earned by keeping customer-outage-minutes below a threshold; grid scale and weather intensity increase by chapter. Win/loss: exceeding the outage-minute threshold or leaving a hospital unpowered beyond its deadline causes defeat; meeting the target advances to the next chapter.
[Must Implement] Load transfer and hop-by-hop cascade propagation; three fault causes and seed-driven thunderstorm corridors; multi-vehicle road-network dispatch and occupied repair time; a verifiable comparison where delayed repair causes significantly more secondary burnouts; a same-seed comparison where capacity expansion significantly reduces cascade size; customer-outage-minute accounting and hospital deadlines, with complete consistency under the same seed and actions.
[Creative Freedom] Nighttime neighborhoods relighting piece by piece, disaster broadcasts, additional disaster types, and citizen-story events are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.

desc: 异能顾客咖啡馆：每位顾客都是全局规则修饰器的经营防线战——减速龟、烤糊狐与雷暴鹦鹉同场叠加，失误喂养一根引爆全店的混乱条
prompt:
[Game] Superpowered-Customer Café Management: Every animal customer arrives with an ability that rewrites the rules of the entire café. A Time Turtle slows all timers, a Fire Fox makes nearby stations burn food more easily, and a Storm Parrot randomly disables equipment. The cooking pipeline and constantly stacking rule modifiers compete in the same space, while every mistake feeds a chaos meter that can explode across the whole shop.
[Core Mechanics] Service pipeline: customers are seated and order dishes; recipes contain multiple steps, each station has its own processing timer, overtime burns food, wrong dishes reduce ratings, and a customer's patience countdown reaching zero makes them leave. Ability modifiers: at least six animal-customer types each apply a global rule modifier while present—for example slowing all timers, shortening nearby burn thresholds, making waiting positions invisible, teleporting seats, or randomly disabling equipment with small storms. Their effects begin when they are present and are removed when they leave; multiple customer abilities stack according to defined rules rather than overwriting one another. Chaos state machine: mistakes add chaos by defined amounts. When the meter fills, the whole café enters an out-of-control mode with more frequent ability triggers and equipment disruption, then returns after cooldown conditions are met. Upgrade economy: income buys faster equipment, more seating, and targeted anti-chaos tools such as a fire-suppression device countering the Fire Fox or a time-stabilizing watch countering the Time Turtle. Tools and abilities form a counter matrix. The day loop lasts at least ten days, unlocking more animals and increasing difficulty. Win/loss: meeting daily targets advances to the next day; rating or funds falling below thresholds causes defeat.
[Must Implement] Complete order → process → serve → patience pipeline; at least six independently observable ability modifiers; defined stacking for simultaneous abilities; a controlled comparison showing that the Time Turtle significantly slows all processing timers while present; chaos accumulation, out-of-control, and recovery state machine; effective counters from anti-chaos tools, with same-seed same-action daily results.
[Creative Freedom] Animal designs and ability presentation, recipe expansion, themed décor, and special-event days are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.

Three-way cascade: weather reduces output → market supply tightens → prices rise, allowing the player to speculate on disaster or suffer major losses. Win/loss loop: daily cycles advance; reaching a legendary asset target or breeding the highest-rarity variety counts as success; bankruptcy or total garden destruction causes defeat.

[Core Mechanics] Daytime economy: citizens commute and produce according to building function, with routes calculated from buildings' actual current positions; daily output generates resources. Three-variable dynamics: stability, citizen mood, and dream energy pull on one another—low mood drags down stability, stability tiers determine nighttime disturbance intensity, and daytime surplus converts proportionally into dream energy. Night disturbances: based on the current stability tier, trigger building displacement, floating road segments, gravity-anomaly zones, and symbolic deformation. Disturbance results persist into the next day—a drifting workshop lengthens commutes and can split production chains. Anchoring: at night, spend dream energy to anchor selected buildings against drift. Too many anchors exhaust dream energy; too few allow economic damage. Imagination axis: disturbances that are tolerated and safely survived generate imagination. At thresholds, unlock surreal buildings with special functions, such as inverted towers or looping bridges. Long-term play moves along a stability axis × imagination axis to multiple endings. Win/loss: stability reaching zero collapses the city and causes defeat; at least three distinct endings are determined by the two axes.
[Must Implement] Commuting based on actual positions and daily economy; bounded interactions among the three variables; disturbance intensity varying by stability tier, with three disturbance types and persistence across days; a controlled comparison showing that failing to anchor a critical building causes significantly larger next-day output loss; surreal-building functions unlocked by imagination must have real effects; at least three endings determined by the two axes, with same-seed same-decision consistency across multiple nights.

prompt:
[Game] 3D Street-Stall Management Simulation: Run a late-night neon barbecue stall where anomalous beings disguise themselves among customers. Hiring one more employee can produce one more meal, while inspecting one more customer can prevent one monster from entering; identification accuracy and service speed compete for the same limited time.

Wages are paid per shift. Identification system: customers are procedurally generated, and anomaly infiltration increases as the night deepens. Clues are semantic-detail differences of at least eight types, such as an impossible shadow direction, missing reflection in the service window, reversed word order when ordering, or abnormal pupils. The player may spend time inspecting a customer and then choose to serve or reject them. Serving an anomaly can result in stolen ingredients, stall damage, or accidents; incorrectly rejecting a normal customer causes bad reviews and reputation loss. Business economy: separate ingredient categories—meat, sauce, vegetables, drinks—deplete and must be replenished by dispatching a courier with travel time; running out of an ingredient stops relevant orders. Peak-flow tides produce customer surges. Tips and reputation depend jointly on serving speed and identification accuracy, and reputation determines next-day traffic and unlocks. The three systems compete: inspecting everyone during a rush collapses the service queue, while inspecting no one lets anomaly losses consume profits; staff scheduling is the main buffer. [Must Implement] Four staff-role behavior chains with hiring and scheduling; at least eight anomaly clues and a complete inspect → decide → consequence loop; ingredient depletion → restock-in-transit → out-of-stock shutdown chain; peak customer surges; reputation jointly determined by identification accuracy and serving speed as a cross-system coupling; daily business resolution and win/loss logic; reproducibility under the same seed and inputs.

[Game] 1v1 Parry Fighter: A scientific fighting arena whose move language is based on quantum-physics concepts. Your opponent is a predictive AI that treats your movement as an equation to solve—every attack and mistake feeds both its prediction model and the arena's entropy meter.
[Core Mechanics] Frame-level fighting core: attacks include high, mid, low, and throws. Precisely timed guards can parry, staggering the opponent, and parry windows are measured in frames. Predictive AI: the AI continuously records the player's movement and attack sequences and updates a model online. At high prediction confidence it proactively intercepts and precisely parries the player. Frequent direction changes and disrupted rhythm reduce confidence, representing uncertainty. When confidence is low, the AI deploys an Entanglement Field—a stationary area where the player's movement direction is mirrored in real time with the AI, removing positional uncertainty and making attacks easy to read. Entropy resource: every whiff or received parry by either side increases a shared entropy meter. When full, either side can unleash Absolute Zero, briefly freezing the opponent in time before a heavy strike, then resetting entropy to zero. As entropy approaches full, the AI may retreat to bait the player into whiffing. The first fighter to deplete the opponent's health wins the round; the match is best-of-three.
[Must Implement] Frame-level guard and parry resolution; online player-behavior modeling with observable confidence changes based on rhythm—repeated patterns are punished while randomized movement reduces accuracy; mirrored movement inside the Entanglement Field and confidence-driven deployment timing; entropy driven only by whiffs and received parries, with full-meter super move and time-freeze resolution; AI retreat-and-bait behavior near full entropy; identical match outcomes under the same seed and input sequence.

[Game] 2D Physics Sumo Duel: Fight an AI wrestler one-on-one in a dohyō with no health bar. Win by pushing the opponent out of bounds or making any body part other than the feet touch the ground. Knockback is not fixed; it is resolved from the real-time momentum difference between both fighters. Your sense of weight comes from physics, while your vulnerabilities come from two hidden meters.
[Core Mechanics] Momentum collision system: each wrestler has mass and real-time velocity. On impact, displacement resolves from the momentum difference—heavier and faster fighters launch lighter and slower fighters farther. High ground friction prevents instant stopping; after impact, wrestlers slide along the floor and decelerate. They can enter a clinch and push against each other, with the direction determined by sustained force and both current states. Balance and stamina system: two hidden meters. Night events are jointly triggered by variable tiers and the seed—for example, low sanity creates an 'island beast sighting' chain, while a large hunting faction can raid the camp and steal supplies. desc: 废墟守夜：查看即喂养威胁的五夜回合生存——电力、噪音、信息三角互斥，每一次看摄像头都在耗电与引怪之间做交易
prompt:
[Game] Industrial-Ruin Night-Watch Text Simulation: You are hired to guard the control room of an abandoned automaton factory for five nights. Electricity is your only budget, while gathering information itself creates noise that feeds threats; every camera check is a trade between power consumption and attracting danger.
[Core Mechanics] Turn-based nights: each night runs from midnight to 6 a.m. in turns, with one command per turn such as viewing a numbered camera, closing or opening the left/right door, turning on a light, or staying silent. Each command has defined power cost and noise generation. Power budget: each night has a fixed battery. When depleted, blackout mode begins and doors and cameras stop functioning. Noise threat: total facility noise accumulates and drives four automatons with distinct behavior along their own routes through a room graph toward the control room; silent turns reduce noise. Incomplete information: at least ten cameras each cover a fixed set of rooms, and automaton positions can be inferred only by checking cameras and sound clues. Checking consumes power and creates noise, making information, electricity, and noise a three-way tradeoff. Closing doors blocks automatons at the threshold but consumes a large amount of power. Starting on the third night, a fifth threat with a different action rule appears. Noise multipliers and automaton speed increase night by night. Win/loss: survive the required turns to finish a night; surviving all five nights wins; any automaton entering the control room causes defeat.
[Must Implement] Command-level power and noise accounting and blackout mode; noise-driven routes for four automatons; camera coverage sets and genuine incomplete information; a controlled comparison showing that frequent camera checks → higher noise → earlier automaton arrival at the doors; survival/attack resolution, with the fifth threat active from night three; turn-by-turn consistency under the same seed and command sequence, and verifiably increasing difficulty across five nights.

prompt:
[Game] Island-Prison Escape Text Simulation: Gull Island Prison claims no one has ever escaped, and you have twelve days. Every daytime action leaves marks in three ledgers—stamina, reputation, and suspicion—while the twelfth night's escape is resolved by a cold deterministic function that enumerates your tool combination and attribute thresholds into freedom or failure.
[Core Mechanics] Action-point economy: stamina as a consumable, reputation as currency, and suspicion as risk each range from 0 to 100. Every day, choose one of three candidate actions such as scouting a ventilation shaft, bribing a guard, working in the cafeteria, or resting in bed. Actions change all three axes by defined amounts and advance the calendar. Underground shop: spend reputation to buy three key tools—a sharpened chisel, guard uniform, and master key. Different tool combinations correspond to different escape routes, whose availability also depends on progress from scouting actions. Resolution engine: on the twelfth night, a deterministic function evaluates tool combination × whether suspicion is below threshold × scouting progress, with multiple routes each having independent success/failure conditions. Two failure thresholds apply throughout: reaching suspicion 100 causes immediate capture that day, while stamina reaching zero causes collapse. Economy and resolution interlock: reputation determines tools, actions determine suspicion, and both feed the final function. Win/loss: successful twelfth-night resolution means escape; capture, collapse, or failed final resolution produce failure endings.
[Must Implement] Three-axis values and daily one-of-three action economy; reputation shop and purchase of three tools; deterministic twelfth-night enumeration with multiple route conditions; a controlled comparison where the same tool combination fails under high suspicion; both failure thresholds always active; complete twelve-day consistency under the same seed and action sequence, with at least one fully replayable winning sequence.

The shadow moves exactly along the trajectory from two seconds earlier, does not collide with the player, and is not blocked by terrain—it is a faithful replay of the past. Many doors can only be opened through self-cooperation by first walking the route and then letting the shadow hold the plate. The player has double jump, wall jump, slide, and dash. prompt:
[Game] Single-Pick Endless Climb: A climber gripping one ice axe with both hands ascends from the mountain foot through atmospheric layers into weightless void. Your swing physics, the mountain's hold generation, and gravity that weakens with altitude rewrite one another, while AI climbers using the same rules compete for the same routes.
[Core Mechanics] Pick physics: both arms and the axe form a physical chain. The axe tip can anchor only to valid wall holds. Once anchored, the body swings around the anchor and accumulates momentum with swing amplitude; pulling the axe free launches the climber toward the next hold. Arm reach limits accessible range, and losing the anchor causes a fall. Procedural generation: the mountain continuously generates upward. Hold density, slope, and surface adhesion become harder with altitude, but every generated segment must pass a reachability check—the distance between adjacent holds may not exceed the reachable limit under current gravity and arm reach. Atmospheric layers: from foothills to void there are at least five bands, with wind and visibility changing by layer and gravity decreasing significantly with altitude. Under low gravity, swing arcs become larger and airtime longer, so the generator correspondingly spaces holds farther apart. AI climbers: use the same axe-body physics as the player, probing, missing, and falling. They have collision volume and compete for the same hold lines, including pushing and crowding. Falling returns the climber to the nearest rest platform. Highest altitude reached is the score, and the climb has no upper end.
[Must Implement] Anchor → swing → release physical chain; continuous hold generation with per-segment reachability verification; gravity decreasing with altitude and simultaneously modifying swing physics and generation parameters (altitude × physics × generator cross-system cascade); AI climbers using the same climbing and collision rules; fall rollback and altitude scoring; stable frame rate and memory during long climbs; same-seed mountain consistency.

Travel disturbances: increasingly dangerous slopes, broken bridges, and mud; rain makes the ground slippery, wind applies sustained force from changing directions, and occasional earthquakes shake footing. prompt:
[Game] Underwater Beat-Navigation Puzzle: A sunken ancient library runs on a looping piece of music. Lights, mechanisms, and sentinel aggression are all attached to the musical timeline. You pilot a small sonar-guided submersible, reading the rhythm and moving with the beat.
[Core Mechanics] Beat timeline: the global looping music is the world clock. The piece is divided into measures; mechanism doors move once every eight measures, lights flash on fixed beats, and musical intensity has at least three layers—calm, middle, climax. Higher intensity increases patrol speed and aggression of eel-like sentinels, with audible and visible warnings before layer transitions. Sonar reveal: the library is normally completely dark. Sonar pulses reveal nearby terrain and entity outlines, which fade after several seconds. Longer charge produces a larger reveal radius. Hull integrity: remaining in open deep-water zones continuously drains integrity; docking in air pockets or behind cover slowly restores it. Sentinel collisions deal large damage. Reaching zero integrity means sinking and failure. Sentinels are sensitive to movement speed: fast targets are chased, while slow movement synchronized to the rhythm is ignored. Puzzles include rotating-ring locks that must align inside specified beat windows to count. Collect at least five data cores and reach the top-floor teleport hall to clear the game. There are at least three regions, with tighter mechanism layouts and denser sentinels in later regions.
[Must Implement] Music timeline driving mechanism movement, light flashes, and tiered sentinel aggression; sonar pulse reveal/fade and charge-based range; integrity drain/recovery/collision resolution and failure; a controlled case where the same movement speed is chased during the climax layer but ignored during a calm layer (music intensity → AI behavior cascade); rotating-ring locks requiring beat-window alignment; data-core collection and completion; same-seed same-action consistency in music loop, mechanism phase, and sentinel scheduling; smooth performance with multiple sentinels and whole-room mechanisms active simultaneously.

desc: 回声深渊：全黑迷宫里看见即暴露——声呐线框显影与循声猎手共用同一套噪音经济
prompt:
[Game] Pitch-Black Maze Sonar Stealth: You are a blind drone trapped in a rotating, transforming underground maze. Sonar pulses illuminate the world as wireframes, but sound is also what hunters track. Seeing has the cost of exposure, so every decibel must be budgeted.
[Core Mechanics] Sound-wave reveal: the entire world is pure black. A pulse expands outward as a wave from the drone, making struck walls and obstacles briefly glow as wireframes before fading. Waves reflect off walls and propagate around corridors, and reveal range scales with pulse loudness. Noise economy: every action generates sound—friction from fast movement, grapple launch and impact, and sonar with loudness tiers determined by charge. Noise propagates through space and attenuates with distance. Sound-hunting enemies: at least two hunters perceive only through hearing, move toward the loudest source within audible range, and search locally. A stationary silent player is effectively nonexistent to them; contact causes defeat. Maze transformation: activating each checkpoint causes several maze blocks to rotate or shift according to preset rules. Memorized paths may close and new ones open. The transformation itself creates a loud sound and briefly attracts hunters. Movement relies on a magnetic grappling hook swinging between walls. Battery charge is a global resource; both sonar and grappling consume energy. Collect three core frequencies and deliver them to the central echo chamber to win; battery depletion or hunter contact causes defeat.
[Must Implement] Sonar-wave expansion, reflection, and temporary fade; tiered noise generation and attenuation; hunters tracking sound sources, searching locally, and causing defeat on contact; louder sonar reveals farther while also alerting hunters from farther away (information ↔ exposure shared-source coupling); checkpoint-triggered block rotation/reassembly; three-frequency collection, delivery resolution, and battery constraint; same-seed same-action consistency for hunter paths and block-transform sequences.
[Creative Freedom] Throwable sound decoys, additional hunter types and block rules, and richer wireframe visualization are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.

prompt:
[Game] Top-Down Infinite Stealth: Every floor is generated on the spot and guaranteed by an internal solver to contain at least one no-alarm route. Guard vision cones and hearing are the only language of the level—you are playing against perception rules inside a maze guaranteed to be solvable.
[Core Mechanics] Guard perception: every guard has a rotating fan-shaped vision cone, hearing radius, and three-state machine—Patrol (walks a route), Suspicious (after hearing noise, stops, turns toward the sound, moves to investigate, then returns to patrol if no target is seen), and Alarm (after directly seeing the player in the cone, persistently pursues; contact causes defeat). There is a visual blind spot directly behind each guard. Stealth model: upright walking is fast but creates a noise circle centered on the player; crouch-walking is slow and silent with a smaller silhouette. A silent takedown is possible only while crouched inside a guard's rear blind spot; a disabled guard is removed from the perception network. Generation and guarantee: each floor procedurally generates walls, cover, and patrol routes, then a solver verifies a route from entrance to exit that never enters a vision cone or triggers suspicion. Failed validation regenerates the floor. Difficulty scaling: every three floors, guard count, cone length, and rotation speed increase by defined gradients. Reaching the exit elevator advances to the next floor indefinitely, with floor count and takedowns scored.
[Must Implement] Vision cones, hearing, three-state transitions, and rear blind spots; walking noise, silent crouching, and rear takedown checks; per-floor generation with solver guarantee of a no-alarm route; exploitable line-of-sight openings created when suspicious guards leave position to investigate (perception → route-opportunity cascade); difficulty gradient every three floors; contact defeat and scoring; same-seed floor layouts.

desc: 双门与床影：呼吸声决定关门还是照灯，床上爬影趁你分身乏术悄悄聚集的卧室夜防
prompt:
[Game] Two-Door Bedroom Night Defense: From midnight to dawn, you are trapped in a bedroom with only left and right doors and a bed. Your only reliable information is sound. Faint breathing behind a door determines whether you should close it or shine the light, while small crawling shadows gather on the bed whenever your attention is elsewhere.
[Core Mechanics] Door threats: the left and right doors independently maintain hidden danger states. When the player approaches a door, that door rerolls its state. If dangerous, after a brief silence it plays faint breathing at a volume significantly lower than other effects, forcing careful listening. At the doorway there are only two actions—shine the light or hold the door closed. Shining the light on a dangerous door causes immediate attack and defeat; holding the dangerous door closed for the required seconds triggers footsteps retreating and clears the danger. On a safe door, shining the light confirms an empty corridor. Bed-creature accumulation: at fixed intervals, one small crawling shadow appears on the bed. At three, the screen begins shaking as a warning. The player must turn back and shine the light on the bed for several seconds to clear the count. Reaching four causes a lethal attack. Positional exclusivity: the player can occupy only the left door, right door, or bed at a time and can handle only one location, while threats at the others continue to evolve. Aggression schedule: the night contains six fixed-duration hourly segments, each increasing danger probability and shortening crawler intervals. Rapid repeated flashlight taps cause a short circuit and disable the light temporarily. Survive all six segments until dawn to win.
[Must Implement] Independent danger rolls for two doors and breathing timing after silence at low volume; immediate defeat for shining light on a dangerous door and successful clearing after holding it closed for the required duration with retreat-footstep feedback; crawler accumulation by interval, warning at three, bed-light clearing, and defeat at four; door threats continuing to evolve while the player guards the bed (position exclusivity → dual-pressure coupling); six-stage aggression escalation; dawn victory and short-circuit penalty; same-seed danger sequence for the whole night.
[Creative Freedom] Spatial/layered sound design, room details and story fragments, and additional distraction events are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.

Collisions create local persistent deformation according to impact speed and angle, and severe impacts can detach parts. Mechanical fault chains: radiator damage causes coolant temperature to keep rising and power to fall after crossing a threshold; an oil-pan leak drains oil and accelerates engine damage; bent suspension creates constant steering pull; tire-pressure damage changes grip and rolling resistance. Faults arise from deformation and misuse and propagate along causal chains. Terrain interaction: asphalt, mud, sand, and gravel each have grip, rolling resistance, and bump characteristics affecting braking, steering, and fault accumulation. Damage rewrites control: deformation and faults change acceleration, top speed, steering response, and straight-line stability in real time, making vehicle condition part of the driving feel. Career challenges: at least five evaluable challenges such as timed traversal below a damage threshold, transporting fragile cargo over specified terrain, or precision parking. Passing unlocks later challenges and vehicles.

desc: 回声噬者：你操纵的是主角三秒前的回声——真身自动前进、敌人盯着双实体、过多回声撕裂时间砸碎场地。
prompt:
[Game] Echo Eater: A control-inverted looping arena where you do not control the protagonist, but their echo from three seconds ago. The real body advances on its own while enemies target both of you, and too many echoes tear time apart and destroy the floor.
[Core Mechanics] Delayed control: player input enters a fixed three-second buffer and is reproduced frame by frame by the echo at the corresponding position. The echo can open doors, pull levers, trigger mechanisms, and attract aggro. Autonomous real body: the real body advances and dodges according to its own rules without direct control. Scene changes caused by the echo—opened doors, triggered mechanisms, diverted enemies—immediately change the real body's viable routes and encounters. Dual-entity reactions: enemies independently target the real body and echoes and can be lured away from the real body. Some enemies track player input patterns and gradually predict movement. Mechanisms treat both entity types identically. Time rifts: if the number of simultaneous echoes exceeds a threshold, a rift permanently destroys one terrain tile. Destroyed areas are impassable to the real body, echoes, and enemies alike. The arena is a procedurally generated sequence of rooms, with Seconds Shards collected as in-run currency for upgrades. Real-body death causes defeat; traversing all rooms wins.
[Must Implement] Fixed three-second input buffering and frame-by-frame echo reproduction; autonomous real-body behavior and real-time response to scene changes made by echoes; differentiated enemy targeting of two entity types and learning of input patterns; excess echoes triggering rifts with identical impassability for all three parties; a cross-system cascade proving that using the echo to change the scene changes the real body's route and survival; identical trajectories in two runs with the same seed and inputs.
[Creative Freedom] Rule-mutating room bosses, glitch-style visual expression, and timed challenge modes are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.
[Mobile] This game targets mobile browsers: choose either portrait or landscape and lock the orientation; all interaction must be touch-only; any hover, keyboard, mouse, or other desktop interaction mentioned in the prompt must be implemented with a touch-equivalent interaction; support mainstream mobile resolutions and safe areas while maintaining smooth performance on mobile devices.

Front lines advance continuously pixel by pixel according to relative force, terrain, and morale, with observable combat in active war zones. Population dynamics: every territory has population, cultural composition, and morale. Population grows over time and determines troop cap and production. Morale affects combat strength, and very low-morale regions risk rebellion. Resource economy: resource-rich zones such as gold, silk, and spices are visibly marked. Resources and population jointly convert into military power and treasury; losing territory immediately loses its population and output. Strategic AI: AI nations evaluate resource zones, weak neighbors, and terrain chokepoints, assemble forces before launching campaigns with explicit objectives, can attack on multiple fronts, and conduct organized retreats when disadvantaged to preserve strength. Hover inspection can show each nation's current war objective and power details. Win by achieving the conquest objective; lose when all national core territory falls.
[Must Implement] Pixel-by-pixel front advancement with terrain modifiers; inspectable population, culture, and morale plus rebellion; resource → population → military conversion and territorial-loss accounting; AI objective selection, concentration, multi-front attacks, retreats, and queryable war goals; win/loss logic; smooth performance with thousands of active frontline pixels and same-seed map consistency.
[Creative Freedom] Diplomacy and alliances, technology, trade routes, and time-speed controls are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.

desc: 时纹回溯战略：花费时纹回到过去改写一道命令，确定性重演引擎从那一刻重写整场战局的未来
prompt:
[Game] Time-Rewind Real-Time Strategy: Two commanders duel on a sandbox battlefield while the entire war is recorded frame by frame as a timeline. Spend rare Time Marks to return to the past and rewrite one order, then the world deterministically replays from that moment to the present—every undo simultaneously rewrites the future of both sides.
[Core Mechanics] Strategy loop: harvest crystal ore and gas, build base facilities, train at least six mutually countering unit types, and destroy the enemy main base to win. Timeline engine: the entire match records every unit and command at fixed simulation steps, and the simulation is fully deterministic so replaying the same timeline produces frame-identical results. Rewind rewrite: spend one Time Mark to jump to any past moment and cancel or add one friendly command. The world immediately replays from that moment to the present under the new command sequence, with differences from the old timeline visualized as residual traces. Causal propagation: edits in the past change all causally downstream events—for example earlier scouting changes intelligence, or a mine raid weakens the opponent's economy—while events without causal connection remain unchanged. Time-Mark economy: relic nodes on the map slowly produce Time Marks. Capturing and holding relics creates a second battlefield, and rewind is impossible without enough marks. Enemy AI commander: fights from visible intelligence, has its own Time-Mark reserve, and can launch counter-rewinds after the player changes key events, creating attack and counterattack through timeline edits.
[Must Implement] Complete harvest → build → train → battle loop with win/loss; global frame-by-frame timeline recording and deterministic replay; causal recomputation after rewind edits and visualized differences; Time-Mark production, consumption, and inability to rewind when insufficient; enemy AI with intelligence-driven warfare and counter-rewinds; full-match replay consistency under same seed and complete command sequence; smooth performance with large numbers of active entities.
[Creative Freedom] Timeline visualization styles, multi-time bookmarks, more units and relic events, and residual-trace aesthetics are unrestricted; original design is encouraged.
[Mobile] This game targets mobile browsers: choose either portrait or landscape and lock the orientation; all interaction must be touch-only; any hover, keyboard, mouse, or other desktop interaction mentioned in the prompt must be implemented with a touch-equivalent interaction; support mainstream mobile resolutions and safe areas while maintaining smooth performance on mobile devices.

[Game] Medieval Battlefield Sandbox: On an open war table, freely place thousands of soldiers and siege engines. Once battle begins, you may watch or take control of any unit group at any time. Victory is not decided only by weapons—morale collapse can spread through formations like a plague.
[Core Mechanics] Battle simulation: at least six unit types—swordsmen, spearmen, archers, cavalry, axemen, and siege engines—have distinct offense, defense, range, and movement, supporting battles with thousands of units. Morale dynamics: every unit has morale. Heavy casualties and flank or rear attacks reduce it. Falling below a threshold triggers rout. Routed soldiers running through dense friendly formations reduce the morale of allies they pass, potentially causing chain collapse. Terrain and weather: high ground boosts ranged units; forests slow cavalry; rain weakens archery and turns low-lying ground into mud, which greatly reduces cavalry charge speed. Deployment and command: before battle, freely place both armies and choose weather. Unused points do not carry over. Card × dice combat: at least 4 card colors each bind to a die type and effect category—heavy melee, ranged burst, defensive block, and support buff. After playing a card, roll the associated die against the card threshold to determine success and effect magnitude; focus can reroll. Hands refill each turn according to draw count. Two-layer durability: damage is applied to shields first, with overflow becoming health loss after shields reach zero. Shields can be restored by defense cards and guarding, while health cannot be healed during the entire battle; a unit at zero health is permanently removed. prompt:
[Game] Living-Motherboard Tower Defense: A roguelike tower defense game on a circuit board that rotates and rearranges itself. Your foundation moves every wave, overclocked firepower creates spreading heat, and that heat can in turn feed certain viruses.
[Core Mechanics] Board movement: the motherboard is grid-based. At the end of each wave, designated blocks rotate or translate in a direction announced one wave in advance. Towers move with their cells, and viruses recalculate paths through the new geometry toward the core. Overclocking and heat: towers can enable overclocking for a large damage boost while continuously adding heat to their cell. Heat spreads into adjacent cells; if cell heat exceeds a threshold, the tower on it burns down. Cooling towers continuously reduce heat in neighboring cells. Include at least 3 virus enemy types that interact with these systems: splitters divide into multiple smaller bodies on death; slowers reduce attack speed of towers within range; heat-eaters absorb heat and become stronger when crossing hot cells. Roguelike layer: at the start of each run, randomly draw modifiers that change numeric rules such as overclock multiplier or rotation frequency. Between runs, loot points unlock permanent upgrades retained across runs and change the next run's initial conditions. Survive all waves with the core alive to win; core health reaching zero is defeat.
[Must Implement] Advance warning and execution of rotation/translation, with enemy repathing through the new geometry; the full overclock damage→heat accumulation→heat spread→burnout→cooling loop; three virus types with distinct mechanics and interactions with heat/towers; both run-specific modifiers and cross-run permanent upgrades; a cross-system cascade where board rearrangement changes cell adjacency and therefore changes heat spread and tower-burn outcomes; identical rotation sequences, waves, and modifier draws under the same seed; smooth performance with hundreds of active units.
[Creative Freedom] Additional virus modifiers, motherboard events such as shorts and surges, and tower-link synergies are unrestricted and encouraged.
[Mobile] This game targets mobile browsers: choose either portrait or landscape orientation and lock it; all interaction must be touch-only throughout. Any hover, keyboard, or mouse interactions mentioned in the prompt must be implemented with touch-equivalent controls. [Game] Wasteland Lighthouse: On a haunted night along the western coast, you are the last keeper of a lighthouse on a lonely cliff. By day, repair the lamp, make oil, and explore wrecks on the beach; by night, light is your only turret—the horde recoils wherever the beam sweeps, and the shape of the shadows becomes the enemy's route of advance.
[Core Mechanics] Lamp-oil economy: during a limited daytime period, allocate work among producing lamp oil, repairing the lighthouse, and upgrading the lens. At night, illumination continuously consumes oil according to its intensity setting; higher settings produce stronger beams but consume more oil. Oil production, consumption, and storage must remain conserved over any time window. Light defense: nighttime hordes advance along multiple routes from the beach toward the lighthouse and civilian shelter. Beam coverage continuously burns and slows monsters. The coverage shape is determined in real time by lens level, orientation, and placeable mirrors. Monsters actively avoid bright light and detour through shadow corridors. Wreck exploration: during the day, explore stranded wrecks to obtain lens parts and cursed weapons; cursed weapons are extremely powerful but have explicit costs, and exploration time directly reduces time available for oil production and repairs. Lights-out rule: if total time with the lighthouse completely dark exceeds a specified limit, a gigantic shadow rises from the sea and launches a devastating attack. Victory/loss: survive all nights with the shelter still standing to win; destruction of the lighthouse core or death of all civilians is defeat, and the number of surviving civilians determines the ending evaluation.
[Must Implement] Daytime time allocation and conserved lamp-oil production/consumption; real-time variable beam coverage with burning and slowing effects; monster pathfinding that avoids light and detours through shadows; wreck exploration combining rewards with curse costs; cumulative lights-out time triggering the giant shadow plus win/loss resolution; identical nighttime horde behavior under the same seed and actions.

prompt:
[Game] Multiplier Army Siege: A portrait-oriented math-gate tower assault. A turret at the bottom automatically emits tiny blue soldiers; when the stream passes through gates labeled with arithmetic operations, the army multiplies. Hundreds to thousands of soft-body soldiers jostle across the battlefield and overwhelm the enemy base at the top.
[Core Mechanics] Math gates: multi-faced gates float across the middle of the battlefield, with faces labeled by operations such as ×2, ×3, or +10. Friendly units crossing a gate are instantly multiplied according to the expression. Some gates are stationary while others slide horizontally back and forth at constant speed. Gate coefficients and enemy spawn rates together define each level's numerical solvability, and the design must guarantee at least one winning positioning strategy. desc: 立国者与血统账本：法律、三币市场与马匹遗传一路传导到骑兵冲锋的十九世纪社会沙盘
prompt:
[Game] Nation Founder: A fictional early-19th-century social sandbox where you establish and govern your own country. Laws and taxes drive AI citizens' livelihoods, three minted currencies float against one another in the market, and the stable's pedigree ledger may be worth more than the treasury—a fine horse's genes propagate all the way into racing, markets, and cavalry charges.
[Core Mechanics] Governance: enact and amend laws covering tax rates, conscription, and citizenship. AI citizens pursue livelihoods according to occupation and behaviorally respond to policy, while AI nations manage their own diplomacy and wars. Three-currency economy: copper, silver, and gold coinage exchange at floating rates determined by supply and demand. International trade settles in different currencies, and market prices emerge from transaction behavior. Horse genetics: every horse has at least 8 attributes such as speed, endurance, and temperament. Offspring inherit from both parents with mutation, pedigree lines remain traceable, and racing events test those traits through performance and prize money. Military and mortality: citizen occupations determine which unit types can be recruited; cavalry combat power is modified by mount attributes. A critically wounded unit enters a rescue countdown: an arriving doctor can save it, but expiration causes permanent death and removal from society. Victory: within a limited number of years, reach a national-power target combining population, wealth, and military strength; lose if the treasury goes bankrupt or the capital falls.
[Must Implement] Law changes producing citizen-behavior and treasury changes; conserved settlement of three floating currencies and international trade; inheritance, breeding, pedigree tracing, and race-based trait testing; propagation of mount attributes into cavalry strength; rescue countdown and permanent death; identical simulation trajectories under the same seed and actions; smooth performance with large numbers of active entities.
[Creative Freedom] Newspapers and letters, additional occupations, diplomatic marriages, and horse-coat collections are unrestricted and encouraged.
[Mobile] This game targets mobile browsers: choose either portrait or landscape orientation and lock it; all interaction must be touch-only throughout. Any hover, keyboard, or mouse interactions mentioned in the prompt must be implemented with touch-equivalent controls. Support mainstream phone resolutions and safe areas while maintaining smooth performance on mobile devices.
